questionText: What is a tariff, and who pays it?
answers: A tax on imported goods, paid by importers and passed on to domestic buyers
A subsidy paid by the government to domestic producers
A limit on the quantity of imports, paid by foreign producers
A tax on exports, paid by domestic producers
explanation: A tariff is a tax on imported goods. Importers hand the money to the government, but they pass the cost on by charging more, so domestic buyers ultimately pay it through a higher price. A quantity limit would be a quota; a payment to producers would be a subsidy.

title: Market for steel
questionText: The diagram shows the domestic market for steel. The country can trade at the world price of $200 per tonne. What quantity of steel is imported?
explanation: At the world price of $200 domestic firms supply 20,000 tonnes while buyers demand 80,000. Imports fill the gap: 80,000 − 20,000 = 60,000 tonnes.

title: Market for steel
questionText: At the world price of $200 per tonne, how much steel is supplied by domestic producers?
explanation: Read across from the world price of $200 to the SUPPLY curve: domestic mills are willing to produce 20,000 tonnes at that price.

title: Market for steel
questionText: At the world price of $200 per tonne, what is the total quantity of steel demanded by domestic buyers?
explanation: Read across from $200 to the DEMAND curve: buyers want 80,000 tonnes in total. Where that steel comes from — domestic mills or imports — is a separate question.

title: Market for steel
questionText: The government now imposes a tariff of $200 per tonne on imported steel. What price do domestic buyers now pay?
explanation: Imported steel now costs the world price plus the tax: $200 + $200 = $400. Domestic mills can charge the same $400, because buyers have no cheaper option. The whole domestic market price rises to $400.

title: Market for steel
questionText: With the $200 tariff in place, how much steel is now produced domestically?
explanation: At the new price of $400, domestic mills move up their supply curve and produce 40,000 tonnes. The supply curve itself does not shift — a tariff taxes imports, it does not change domestic costs.

title: Market for steel
questionText: By how much does domestic steel production rise as a result of the tariff?
explanation: Domestic production rises from 20,000 tonnes at $200 to 40,000 tonnes at $400 — an increase of 20,000 tonnes. This gain to domestic producers is the usual justification for a tariff.

title: Market for steel
questionText: With the $200 tariff in place, what quantity of steel is now imported?
explanation: At $400, buyers demand 60,000 tonnes and domestic mills supply 40,000. Imports are squeezed to the remaining gap: 60,000 − 40,000 = 20,000 tonnes.

title: Market for steel
questionText: By how much do steel imports fall as a result of the tariff?
explanation: Imports fall from 60,000 to 20,000 tonnes — a drop of 40,000. Notice this comes from both directions at once: domestic production rose 20,000 AND total demand fell 20,000. Imports get squeezed from both ends.

title: Market for steel
questionText: By how much does the total quantity of steel bought fall as a result of the tariff?
explanation: Total demand contracts along the demand curve from 80,000 tonnes at $200 to 60,000 tonnes at $400 — a fall of 20,000 tonnes. A tariff makes buyers worse off: they get less steel and pay more for it.

title: Market for steel
questionText: How much tariff revenue does the government collect?
explanation: The government collects the tax only on steel that is actually imported — not on domestic output. Imports after the tariff are 20,000 tonnes: $200 × 20,000 = $4 million. Using the pre-tariff import quantity is the classic trap here.

title: Market for wheat
questionText: The diagram shows the domestic market for wheat, which trades at the world price of $60 per tonne. What quantity of wheat is imported?
explanation: At the world price of $60 domestic farmers supply 15,000 tonnes while buyers demand 35,000. Imports fill the gap: 35,000 − 15,000 = 20,000 tonnes.

title: Market for wheat
questionText: The government wants to cut wheat imports from 20,000 to 10,000 tonnes. What per-unit tariff is required?
explanation: Work out the price that leaves a 10,000 tonne gap. At $80 domestic supply is 20,000 tonnes and demand is 30,000, leaving imports of exactly 10,000. Getting the price from $60 to $80 needs a tariff of $20 per tonne.

title: Market for wheat
questionText: With the $20 tariff in place, what price do domestic wheat buyers now pay?
explanation: Imported wheat now costs $60 + $20 = $80 per tonne, and domestic wheat sells for the same $80.

title: Market for wheat
questionText: After the tariff, what is the total revenue earned by domestic wheat producers?
explanation: At $80, domestic farmers produce 20,000 tonnes and sell every tonne at $80: $80 × 20,000 = $1.6 million. They receive the full tariff-inflated price — they do not pay the tariff, only importers do.

title: Market for wheat
questionText: How much tariff revenue does the government collect on imported wheat?
explanation: The tariff is collected only on imports, which are now 10,000 tonnes: $20 × 10,000 = $200,000. The government does not collect anything on the 20,000 tonnes grown domestically.

title: Market for cars
questionText: The diagram shows the domestic market for cars, which trades at the world price of $15,000. Before any tariff, what is the total revenue of domestic car producers? (domestic output x price)
explanation: At the world price of $15,000 domestic firms produce 30,000 cars: 30,000 × $15,000 = $450 million.

title: Market for cars
questionText: What size tariff per car would the government need to impose to eliminate car imports entirely?
explanation: Imports vanish only when domestic supply meets domestic demand unaided — the closed-market equilibrium at $25,000, where both are 50,000 cars. Getting the price from $15,000 up to $25,000 needs a tariff of $10,000 per car.

title: Market for cars
questionText: The government instead imposes a $5,000 tariff per car, raising the price to $20,000. What is the total revenue of domestic car producers now? (domestic output x price)
explanation: At $20,000 domestic firms produce 40,000 cars: 40,000 × $20,000 = $800 million. Their revenue rises for two reasons at once — a higher price AND a larger quantity.

title: Market for cars
questionText: By how much has the revenue of domestic car producers changed as a result of the $5,000 tariff?
explanation: Revenue rises from $450 million to $800 million: an increase of $350 million. That gain is why domestic producers lobby for tariffs — though it comes at the expense of buyers, who pay $5,000 more per car and buy fewer of them.
